Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: A friend who has just started assembling furniture asks for a quick video call because the instructions are confusing.
Expectation2: Arrive on time for scheduled volunteer shifts
Situation2: Several other volunteers can easily cover the first part of the shift if someone shows up a little late.
Story: My phone buzzed just as I was about to leave for my volunteer shift at the community center. It was Sam, my oldest friend, sounding frazzled. “Hey, can you hop on a quick video call? I’m drowning in these furniture instructions and I really need your help.” I glanced at the clock. My shift started in twenty minutes, but I knew the center would be fine if I was a little late—there were always plenty of volunteers at the start. Still, I’d promised myself I’d be reliable, and I hated the idea of letting the team down. But Sam rarely asked for help, and I could hear the frustration in his voice. I felt torn, caught between being the dependable volunteer and the supportive friend. My heart raced as I weighed the guilt of possibly letting down my team against the worry of leaving Sam to struggle alone. I stared at my phone, feeling the pressure of both expectations closing in, unsure which role I should choose in this moment.
